elements.name: Fixed Allocation
elements.what: Pre-allocate all objects and buffers during initialization so no dynamic allocation happens at runtime.
elements.problem: Dynamic allocation can fail unpredictably and fragment memory; pre-allocating everything up front guarantees the program can never run out of memory mid-operation.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Variable Allocation
elements.what: Allocate and deallocate variable-sized objects on demand from a heap as the program needs them.
elements.problem: Fixed pre-allocation wastes memory on empty reserved space; allocating only what is needed, when needed, avoids unused headroom at the cost of allocation failure handling and fragmentation.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Pooled Allocation
elements.what: Pre-allocate a pool of same-sized blocks or objects and recycle them, allocating and freeing in constant time with zero fragmentation.
elements.problem: Allocating a large number of similar objects from a general heap is slow and fragments memory; a pool of recycled fixed-size blocks makes allocation deterministic and bounded.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Memory Discard
elements.what: Allocate temporary objects from a temporary workspace and reclaim them all at once by discarding the whole workspace.
elements.problem: Freeing many short-lived temporaries individually is slow and error-prone; discarding an entire scratch region on completion reclaims everything in one cheap operation.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Compaction
elements.what: Move live objects together in memory to squeeze out the unused gaps between them, recovering memory lost to fragmentation.
elements.problem: Long-running allocation and deallocation leaves free memory scattered in unusable fragments; relocating objects (usually via handles or indirection) coalesces free space into allocatable blocks.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Packed Data
elements.what: Pack data items within a structure (bit-fields, smaller types, eliminated padding) so they occupy minimum space.
elements.problem: Naturally-aligned, full-width representations waste scarce RAM; packing trades access cost for a smaller memory footprint.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Sharing
elements.what: Store one copy of identical information and reference it from everywhere it is needed instead of duplicating it.
elements.problem: Multiple copies of the same data multiply memory cost; sharing a single instance removes the duplication at the price of managing shared ownership and mutation (closely related to GoF Flyweight).
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Copy-on-Write
elements.what: Share an object between clients until one needs to modify it, then transparently copy it and let the writer mutate the private copy.
elements.problem: Eager copying wastes memory and time when most copies are never modified; deferring the copy to first write keeps sharing cheap while preserving value semantics.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Embedded Pointer
elements.what: Embed the pointers that maintain a collection directly into each member object instead of allocating external link nodes.
elements.problem: External link nodes double the allocation count and memory overhead of collections; embedding the links in the objects removes per-node allocations (the intrusive-container idiom).
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Multiple Representations
elements.what: Provide several implementations of an object, each optimized for different size/speed trade-offs, behind one common interface.
elements.problem: One representation cannot be optimal for all instances (small vs large, read-only vs mutable); switching representations per instance keeps memory minimal without changing clients.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Paging
elements.what: Keep code and data on secondary storage and move fixed-size pages in and out of main memory on demand, giving the illusion of more memory.
elements.problem: The working set exceeds physical RAM; paging trades access latency for effectively unbounded addressable data (the OS virtual-memory realization is the system-level cousin).
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Read-Only Memory
elements.what: Place read-only code and constant data in ROM/flash rather than RAM, reserving scarce writable memory for mutable state.
elements.problem: RAM is the scarcest memory on small systems while ROM/flash is comparatively plentiful; segregating immutable content into read-only memory frees RAM.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Hooks
elements.what: Access read-only information through hooks (pointers or jump slots) held in writable storage, so changing the hooks gives the illusion of changing ROM content.
elements.problem: Information baked into ROM cannot be updated in the field; a small writable indirection layer allows patching and extension without rewriting read-only storage.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Memory Limit
elements.what: Set an explicit memory budget for each component and fail allocations that would exceed the component's limit.
elements.problem: Competing components can starve each other of memory unpredictably; enforced per-component limits contain failures and make memory use plannable.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)
elements.borderline: Closer to a budgeting policy than a code mechanism, but pattern-cataloged and implemented via allocator quota checks - kept IN.

elements.name: Captain Oates
elements.what: On memory pressure, have less vital components voluntarily sacrifice their memory (caches, optional buffers) so more important tasks can proceed.
elements.problem: When memory runs out, failing the currently-allocating (possibly critical) task is the wrong victim choice; deliberately releasing low-value memory first preserves the vital functions.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Data Files
elements.what: Process data a little at a time from secondary storage, keeping only the current working portion in main memory.
elements.problem: Data sets that do not fit in RAM cannot be loaded whole; incremental streaming bounds the memory footprint regardless of data size.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Resource Files
elements.what: Keep configuration data and read-only resources in files on secondary storage, loading and discarding each item as needed.
elements.problem: Keeping all configuration and UI resources resident wastes RAM and hard-codes content; externalized, demand-loaded resources cut memory use and ease localization/updates.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Compression
elements.what: Store data in a compressed representation in memory or storage, decompressing on access, to fit more data in less space.
elements.problem: Bulk data exceeds available memory; compression trades CPU time for footprint. Noble & Weir's specializations (Table Compression, Difference Coding, Adaptive Compression) are folded here as variants per the no-algorithm-zoo rule.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Super Loop
elements.what: Structure the whole application as one endless main loop that calls each task function in turn, with ISRs as the only asynchronous activity.
elements.problem: Tiny systems need multitask-like behavior without the cost and complexity of an RTOS; a single repeating loop plus interrupts is the minimal, fully deterministic executive.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Time-Triggered Co-operative Scheduler
elements.what: Dispatch short run-to-completion tasks from a timer-tick-driven table at fixed periods and offsets, with no preemption between tasks.
elements.problem: Preemptive kernels bring race conditions and jitter that are hard to certify; a cooperative tick-driven dispatcher gives highly predictable timing provided every task's duration stays under the tick. Pont's hybrid (TTH) variant, allowing one preemptive task, is folded here.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Multi-State Task
elements.what: Implement a long-running activity as a state machine that advances one short step per scheduler invocation instead of blocking or busy-waiting.
elements.problem: A cooperative scheduler cannot tolerate tasks that block or run long; decomposing the activity into per-tick states keeps every invocation short and the schedule predictable.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Loop Timeout
elements.what: Bound every polling/wait loop with a software counter or hardware timer so the loop cannot hang forever if the awaited hardware condition never occurs.
elements.problem: Unbounded waits on hardware flags hang the whole system when a peripheral fails; an explicit timeout converts a hang into a detectable, handleable error. Pont's HARDWARE TIMEOUT timer-based variant is folded here.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Sandwich Delay
elements.what: Wrap a code section between a hardware-timer start and a wait-for-timer end so the section always consumes the same wall-clock duration regardless of path taken.
elements.problem: Variable execution paths introduce task jitter that degrades time-triggered control and sampling quality; padding every path to a fixed duration with a timer equalizes timing.
elements.named_in: Meeting Real-Time Constraints Using 'Sandwich Delays' - Pont, Kurian & Bautista (EuroPLoP 2006)

elements.name: Cyclic Executive
elements.what: Execute a fixed, precomputed sequence of task frames (minor cycles within a repeating major cycle) driven by a periodic timer, with no runtime scheduling decisions.
elements.problem: Hard-real-time certification favors fully static, analyzable timing; a table of frames laid out offline guarantees every deadline by construction at the cost of scheduling flexibility.
elements.named_in: The Cyclic Executive Model and Ada - Baker & Shaw (Real-Time Systems, 1989)

elements.name: Schedule Table
elements.what: A statically configured table of expiry points on a counter, each releasing tasks or setting events at fixed offsets, cyclically or once, as an OS-level time-triggered dispatch mechanism.
elements.problem: Periodic activations with precise relative phasing are clumsy to build from individual alarms; a schedule table expresses the whole time-triggered activation pattern declaratively and synchronizably (e.g. to a global time base).
elements.named_in: AUTOSAR Specification of Operating System (schedule tables); OSEK/VDX time-triggered OS

elements.name: Tickless Idle
elements.what: Suppress the periodic scheduler tick during idle, program a one-shot wakeup for the next deadline, and sleep the CPU in a low-power mode until then.
elements.problem: A free-running tick interrupt wakes the CPU pointlessly and dominates power draw in mostly-idle systems; eliminating idle ticks lets the MCU stay in deep sleep between real events.
elements.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (tickless idle mode)

elements.name: Watchdog Timer
elements.what: A hardware countdown timer that resets the system unless the software periodically restarts ('kicks') it, forcing recovery from hangs; windowed variants also reject too-early kicks.
elements.problem: Firmware can lock up from bugs, EMI, or deadlock with no operator present; an independent timer guarantees the system returns to a known state. Multi-task supervision schemes (each task must check in before the kick) extend coverage to partial hangs.
elements.named_in: Better Embedded System Software - Koopman (2010)

elements.name: Debounce
elements.what: Filter the mechanical bounce of switches/inputs by accepting a state change only after it remains stable for a defined time or vote count.
elements.problem: Mechanical contacts chatter for milliseconds on every actuation, producing spurious edges; time- or counter-based filtering turns the noisy signal into one clean logical event.
elements.named_in: A Guide to Debouncing - Jack Ganssle (2004)

elements.name: ISR with Deferred Work
elements.what: Keep the interrupt service routine minimal (acknowledge, capture data, set a flag/queue item) and defer the bulk of the processing to task/thread context.
elements.problem: Long ISRs blow interrupt latency budgets and block lower-priority interrupts; splitting urgent hardware handling from deferrable processing keeps the system responsive and analyzable.
elements.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

elements.name: Nested Interrupt Handling
elements.what: Allow a higher-priority interrupt to preempt a running lower-priority ISR by re-enabling interrupts (or relying on NVIC priority hardware) inside handlers.
elements.problem: With nesting disabled, a slow low-priority ISR delays urgent interrupts past their deadlines; controlled nesting bounds latency for critical sources at the cost of stack depth and reentrancy discipline.
elements.named_in: The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 Processors - Yiu (2013)

elements.name: Interrupt Vector Table
elements.what: A table of handler entry addresses, indexed by exception/interrupt number, through which the CPU dispatches to the right ISR; firmware populates and sometimes relocates it (e.g. VTOR).
elements.problem: Hardware must find the correct handler in bounded time for any interrupt source; a fixed-layout dispatch table is the universal mechanism, and its relocation underlies bootloaders and RAM-vectored systems.
elements.named_in: The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 Processors - Yiu (2013)
elements.borderline: Hardware-defined structure at the floor of the design band - kept IN per charter as the named dispatch construct firmware designs around.

elements.name: Interrupt-Masking Critical Section
elements.what: Protect data shared between mainline code and ISRs by briefly disabling (or priority-masking) interrupts around the access.
elements.problem: An interrupt arriving mid-update leaves shared data half-written (the shared-data problem); masking interrupts for a short bounded window makes the access atomic on a uniprocessor.
elements.named_in: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)
elements.borderline: Overlaps the general critical-section element owned by the synchronization scout; kept for its ISR-specific form and naming.

elements.name: Priority Inheritance
elements.what: When a low-priority task holds a lock a high-priority task needs, temporarily boost the holder to the waiter's priority until it releases the lock.
elements.problem: Unbounded priority inversion lets a medium-priority task starve a high-priority one blocked on a low-priority lock holder (the Mars Pathfinder failure); inheritance bounds the inversion to the critical section length.
elements.named_in: Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization - Sha, Rajkumar & Lehoczky (IEEE Trans. Computers, 1990)

elements.name: Priority Ceiling Protocol
elements.what: Assign each lock a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that uses it, and run (or admit) lockers at that ceiling, preventing deadlock and chained blocking.
elements.problem: Priority inheritance alone still permits deadlock and multiple blocking; ceiling protocols guarantee at most one blocking interval and no mutex deadlock, at the cost of static lock-usage knowledge.
elements.named_in: Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization - Sha, Rajkumar & Lehoczky (IEEE Trans. Computers, 1990)

elements.name: Protothreads
elements.what: Extremely lightweight stackless thread abstraction for C that gives event-driven code a sequential blocking-style structure, implemented with switch-based local continuations.
elements.problem: Event-driven state-machine code obscures control flow while real threads cost a stack each; protothreads express sequential waits in ~2 bytes of state per thread on memory-constrained MCUs.
elements.named_in: Protothreads: Simplifying Event-Driven Programming of Memory-Constrained Embedded Systems - Dunkels et al. (2006)

elements.name: Double-Buffered DMA
elements.what: Configure the DMA controller with two memory buffers (or one circular buffer with half/full-transfer interrupts) so hardware fills one while software processes the other, swapping automatically at each transfer end.
elements.problem: A single DMA buffer forces software to drain it in real time or lose data; hardware-managed buffer alternation decouples transfer from processing and removes the hard servicing deadline.
elements.named_in: AN4031 - Using the STM32F2, STM32F4 and STM32F7 Series DMA controller (STMicroelectronics)

elements.name: Ping-Pong Buffer
elements.what: Two buffers alternate roles between a producer and a consumer: while one is being filled the other is processed, and the roles swap on completion.
elements.problem: A producer (ISR, DMA, sampling loop) and consumer working in one buffer corrupt or lose data; alternating disjoint buffers lets both proceed concurrently on different memory. Kept distinct from double-buffered DMA: ping-pong is the general software-role-swap mechanism, DMA double-buffering its hardware-managed realization.
elements.named_in: Ping Pong Buffers - Embedded.fm (White, 2017); Microchip DMA 'Ping-Pong Mode' documentation

elements.name: Scatter-Gather DMA
elements.what: Program the DMA controller with a chain of descriptors so one logical transfer moves data to/from multiple non-contiguous memory regions without CPU intervention between segments.
elements.problem: Data often lives in scattered buffers (protocol headers + payload, page-fragmented memory); descriptor chains avoid copying into one contiguous bounce buffer and avoid per-segment CPU servicing.
elements.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

elements.name: Polled I/O
elements.what: The CPU repeatedly reads a device status register and transfers data itself when the device is ready, instead of using interrupts or DMA.
elements.problem: Interrupt machinery adds latency variance, complexity, and reentrancy hazards that tiny or timing-critical drivers may not want; polling is simple and deterministic at the cost of busy CPU time.
elements.named_in: Polling (computer science) - Wikipedia

elements.name: Bit Banging
elements.what: Implement a communications protocol entirely in software by directly toggling and sampling GPIO pins with timed code, instead of using dedicated peripheral hardware.
elements.problem: The MCU lacks (or has run out of) hardware controllers for a needed protocol; software-timed pin manipulation trades CPU load and timing precision for hardware independence.
elements.named_in: Bit banging - Wikipedia

elements.name: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing
elements.what: Encode packets so the frame delimiter byte never appears in the payload, with a small, fixed worst-case overhead, enabling unambiguous packet boundaries on byte streams.
elements.problem: Classic escape-based byte stuffing (SLIP/HDLC) can double packet size in the worst case, which breaks buffer and bandwidth budgets; COBS bounds overhead to one byte per 254 while keeping delimiter-free payloads.
elements.named_in: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing - Cheshire & Baker (IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 1999)

elements.name: Memory-Mapped Register Access
elements.what: Address peripheral hardware registers as (volatile-qualified) memory locations through typed pointers or structure overlays, with disciplined read/write ordering.
elements.problem: Peripherals must be controlled from portable C/C++ without compiler-reordered or elided accesses; the volatile-pointer/struct-overlay discipline (plus hardware aids like Cortex-M bit-banding for atomic bit access) is the canonical mechanism.
elements.named_in: Dan Saks embedded.com columns on memory-mapped devices in C and C++

elements.name: Shadow Register
elements.what: Maintain a RAM copy of a hardware register's intended contents, perform all read-modify-write logic on the copy, and write the whole copy to the device.
elements.problem: Write-only registers cannot be read back and read-modify-write on live registers races with hardware (the PIC RMW problem); a software shadow makes register state knowable and updates atomic. Vendors also use 'shadow register' for hardware-buffered registers that latch atomically (e.g. PWM compare shadows) - noted as the hardware sense.
elements.named_in: Shadow Register - ScienceDirect Topics (Elsevier embedded-systems references); PIC/AVR vendor documentation

elements.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer
elements.what: A stable set of interfaces that isolates application and middleware code from register-level hardware detail, so the same firmware runs across MCUs by swapping the layer beneath.
elements.problem: Register-level code welds the application to one chip; a defined abstraction boundary makes firmware portable, testable off-target, and reusable across product lines.
elements.named_in: Reusable Firmware Development: A Practical Approach to APIs, HALs and Drivers - Beningo (2017)
elements.borderline: Layering shades toward architecture; kept IN as an implementable interface construct within one firmware program, with the layered-firmware-architecture reading parked for Phase 3.

elements.name: Bootloader Jump / Handoff
elements.what: A small boot program validates the application image, then hands off execution by loading the application's stack pointer and reset vector (relocating the vector table) and jumping to it with hardware in a known state.
elements.problem: Field-updatable and multi-image devices need a trusted first stage that can select, verify, and start an application image; the disciplined SP/PC/vector handoff is the mechanism that makes the transition safe and restartable.
elements.named_in: From Zero to main(): How to Write a Bootloader from Scratch - Memfault Interrupt (2019)

elements.name: A/B Firmware Image Update
elements.what: Keep two firmware image slots; write the new image into the inactive slot, verify it, then atomically switch the boot selection, keeping the old image as instant fallback.
elements.problem: In-place firmware updates brick the device on power loss or a bad image; dual slots make updates atomic and reversible. Golden-image recovery slots, anti-rollback counters, and delta updates are folded here as variants.
elements.named_in: Device Firmware Update Cookbook - Memfault Interrupt

elements.name: EEPROM Emulation in Flash
elements.what: Emulate byte-updatable EEPROM semantics on page-erasable flash by journaling variable records across reserved pages and swapping/compacting pages when full.
elements.problem: Many MCUs lack true EEPROM while flash only erases in large pages with limited endurance; record journaling plus page rotation provides small-datum persistence with wear spreading and power-loss recovery.
elements.named_in: AN2594 - EEPROM emulation in STM32F10x microcontrollers (STMicroelectronics)

elements.name: Flash Wear Leveling
elements.what: Distribute writes and erases evenly across flash pages/blocks (via remapping or rotation) so no single block exhausts its limited erase endurance prematurely.
elements.problem: Flash blocks endure only a bounded number of erase cycles while write traffic is naturally skewed to hot data; leveling the wear multiplies effective device lifetime.
elements.named_in: Wear leveling - Wikipedia; AN798 EEPROM Emulation with Wear-Leveling (Silicon Labs)

elements.name: Memory Overlay
elements.what: Divide a program into sections that share the same memory region, loading each overlay from secondary storage into the shared region only when its code/data is needed.
elements.problem: The program is larger than the memory it must run in; time-multiplexing one region among mutually exclusive sections fits large programs into small RAM, predating and paralleling virtual memory.
elements.named_in: Linkers and Loaders - Levine (1999)

elements.name: Stack Painting / Watermarking
elements.what: Fill each stack with a known pattern at startup and later scan for the deepest overwritten address to measure worst-case stack usage and detect near-overflow.
elements.problem: Stack overflow in fixed-stack embedded systems corrupts adjacent memory silently; painting makes actual usage observable so stack sizes can be right-sized and overflows caught (complementary to canary/guard-zone checks).
elements.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (stack overflow detection and uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark)

elements.name: Brown-Out Handling
elements.what: Detect supply voltage sagging below a safe threshold (via an on-chip or external detector) and hold the MCU in reset or run a controlled shutdown until power is reliable.
elements.problem: During sags the CPU and flash misbehave unpredictably (corrupted writes, erratic execution) without a clean power-off; explicit brown-out detection converts an undefined-behavior region into a defined reset or safe-save path.
elements.named_in: AVR180: External Brown-out Protection - Atmel/Microchip application note

elements.name: Safe State
elements.what: A predefined operating condition without unreasonable risk that the system deliberately enters on fault detection (outputs de-energized, actuators parked, subsystem disabled).
elements.problem: When a fault makes continued normal operation untrustworthy, the firmware needs a designed, reachable state that minimizes harm; defining and driving to that state is the core functional-safety mechanism.
elements.named_in: ISO 26262:2018 - Road vehicles - Functional safety
elements.borderline: A system-safety concept as much as a code mechanism, but implemented as a concrete in-program transition routine - kept IN with the tag.

elements.name: Built-In Self-Test
elements.what: Firmware routines that exercise and verify the system's own hardware (RAM patterns, ROM checksums, register/ALU checks, peripheral loopbacks) at startup or periodically.
elements.problem: Latent hardware faults otherwise surface only as mysterious runtime failures; explicit self-tests detect them at a moment the system can still report, refuse to run, or fail safe. RAM march tests and ROM CRC checks are folded here as variants.
elements.named_in: Built-in self-test - Wikipedia

elements.name: Program Sequence Monitoring
elements.what: Instrument checkpoints along required execution paths and have a monitor (often the watchdog manager) verify that checkpoints occur in the legal order and cadence.
elements.problem: A timing watchdog alone cannot detect code that runs on time but in the wrong order (skipped safety checks, corrupted control flow); sequence monitoring detects illegal execution paths.
elements.named_in: IEC 61508-7:2010 - program sequence monitoring technique

elements.name: CRC Integrity Check
elements.what: Append a cyclic-redundancy-check value to data (messages, firmware images, config blocks, RAM copies) and verify it on receipt or use to detect corruption.
elements.problem: Bit errors from noisy links, failing flash, or memory corruption must be detected with high probability and low cost; CRCs give strong, cheap error detection (polynomial choice per Koopman's CRC selection work; Douglass catalogs it as the CRC Pattern).
elements.named_in: A Painless Guide to CRC Error Detection Algorithms - Ross Williams (1993)

elements.name: Lookup Table
elements.what: Replace runtime computation with indexing into a precomputed table of results, optionally interpolating between entries for continuous functions.
elements.problem: Transcendental math, calibration curves, and CRC steps are too slow (or need an FPU) on small CPUs; trading ROM for computation gives constant-time, deterministic evaluation.
elements.named_in: Lookup table - Wikipedia

elements.name: Fixed-Point Arithmetic
elements.what: Represent fractional values as scaled integers with an implicit binary point (Qm.n), doing real-number math with integer instructions.
elements.problem: Floating point is slow, large, or absent on many MCUs/DSPs and complicates certification; fixed-point gives fast deterministic fractional math at the cost of explicit range/precision management.
elements.named_in: Embedded Systems Building Blocks - Labrosse (fixed-point math chapter)

elements.name: Saturation Arithmetic
elements.what: Arithmetic in which results exceeding the representable range clamp to the minimum/maximum value instead of wrapping around.
elements.problem: Two's-complement wraparound turns small overflows into catastrophic sign flips in control and signal paths; saturating operations (often single DSP instructions) degrade gracefully at range limits.
elements.named_in: Saturation arithmetic - Wikipedia

parked_architecture.name: Application Switching (Noble & Weir)
parked_architecture.why: Splits the system into independent executables run one at a time - a statement of system-level structure, not an in-program mechanism (fails altitude test upward).

parked_architecture.name: Time-Triggered Architecture (Kopetz)
parked_architecture.why: System/network-level computation and communication architecture (TTA, TTP); the in-program TTC scheduler element is cataloged, the architecture goes to Phase 3 (corpus: kopetzbauer).

parked_architecture.name: Spatial/temporal partitioning (ARINC 653 / IMA)
parked_architecture.why: Platform-level isolation architecture between applications; MPU/MMU enforcement is configuration of system structure (corpus: arinc653, rushby).

parked_architecture.name: Layered firmware architecture (driver/HAL/middleware/application)
parked_architecture.why: The layering itself is architectural structure; only the HAL interface construct was kept as a borderline design element (corpus: lacamera, beningodesign).

parked_architecture.name: Redundant channel structures (TMR, dual-channel 1oo2, homogeneous/heterogeneous redundancy)
parked_architecture.why: Replication topologies across channels/processors are system-level fault-tolerance structure (Douglass channel patterns; IEC 61508).

parked_architecture.name: Limp-home / degraded mode operation
parked_architecture.why: System-level behavioral policy for continuing service under fault (automotive lexicon); the in-program safe-state transition is cataloged instead.

parked_architecture.name: Board support package (BSP)
parked_architecture.why: A packaging/structural unit organizing platform code, not a mechanism implementable inside one component.

excluded_notable.name: Small Interfaces (Noble & Weir)
excluded_notable.why: API-design guidance ('let clients control data transfer') rather than an implementable mechanism; flagged for the construction-api scout to reconsider.

excluded_notable.name: Packages (Noble & Weir)
excluded_notable.why: Deployment/dynamic-loading granularity - realized by OS loader machinery, below/aside the design band as a program-internal mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Reference Counting (Noble & Weir chapter pattern)
excluded_notable.why: Genuine element, deliberately ceded to the resource-management scout (general, not embedded-specific) to avoid cross-scout duplication; N&W is a naming source if needed.

excluded_notable.name: Garbage Collection (Noble & Weir chapter pattern)
excluded_notable.why: Same as reference counting - general resource-management territory; recorded here so the fold is not silent.

excluded_notable.name: Rate-monotonic / earliest-deadline-first scheduling policies
excluded_notable.why: Named scheduling algorithms with analysis theory (Liu & Layland, corpus liulayland) - algorithm/analysis level; flagged for the scheduling scout's policy call.

excluded_notable.name: Linker-script section placement (attribute/section control, KEEP, memory regions)
excluded_notable.why: Toolchain mechanism below the design band (corpus ld, zephyrlinker); recurring but tool-configuration rather than program design.

excluded_notable.name: Semihosting / RTT debug channels
excluded_notable.why: Debug/tooling infrastructure (corpus semihosting, segger), not a design mechanism of the shipped program.

excluded_notable.name: volatile qualifier discipline
excluded_notable.why: Raw language-syntax level; folded as a note into memory-mapped register access (see eideregehr for the miscompilation literature).

excluded_notable.name: Execute-in-place (XIP)
excluded_notable.why: Platform memory-configuration choice (run code directly from flash) rather than an in-program mechanism; recorded for completeness.

excluded_notable.name: MPU-based task/memory isolation (FreeRTOS-MPU style)
excluded_notable.why: Named mostly in RTOS/vendor docs; the partitioning concept parked at architecture (ARINC 653 entry), the per-task MPU configuration judged platform setup rather than a design element - honest borderline exclusion.

excluded_notable.name: DMA cache-coherence maintenance (clean/invalidate discipline)
excluded_notable.why: Real recurring discipline (LDD3, ARM docs) but a hardware-correctness protocol tied to cache architecture; left for the OS/systems scout to weigh.

notes: Coverage: full Noble & Weir Small Memory Software catalog enumerated and verified live from the book's own PatternSummaries.pdf (correction vs charter brief: there is no 'Partial Failure' pattern in the catalog; Small Architecture = Memory Limit, Small Interfaces, Captain Oates, Read-Only Memory, Hooks). Pont PTTES core pattern names (SUPER LOOP, CO-OPERATIVE SCHEDULER, MULTI-STATE TASK, LOOP TIMEOUT, HARDWARE WATCHDOG) verified from Pont's own JSS 2002 case-study paper; SANDWICH DELAY verified via the EuroPLoP 2006 paper. Dedup decisions: ping-pong buffer (software role swap) kept distinct from double-buffered DMA (hardware pointer swap, AN4031) with cross-notes; TTH hybrid scheduler folded into TTC; HARDWARE TIMEOUT folded into LOOP TIMEOUT; POST and RAM/ROM tests folded into BIST; windowed and software/task-supervision watchdogs folded into watchdog timer; bit-banding folded into memory-mapped register access; golden image/anti-rollback/delta update folded into A/B update; Table/Difference/Adaptive Compression folded into Compression; foreground/background system folded into super loop as aka. Deliberate cessions to sibling scouts (recorded, not silent): circular/ring buffer, message queue/mailbox, event loop, active object, semaphores/mutexes/event groups, software timers/timer wheel, reference counting, garbage collection, object pool (general), state machine implementations, stack canary (security scout). White (white) and Koopman (koopmanbess) were harvested via their signature mechanisms (watchdog, stack watermarking, CRC, brownout, ping-pong/DMA buffering, HAL) rather than an independent chapter-by-chapter ToC sweep - residual thin spot. Beningo (beningofw) yielded only HAL: his driver-model taxonomy (polling/interrupt/DMA driver variants) has names too weak to pass the establishedness gate.
